automation account for about 28% of employment” (Lassebie & 
Quintini, 2022, p. 42). 
Felten, Raj, and Seamans (2021) began with 10 AI applications 
based on “categories defined and described by the Electronic Frontier

Foundation (EFF) AI Progress Measurement project” (Felten, Raj, and 
Seamans, 2021, p. 2198). They linked these applications to the 52 
O*NET abilities, generating a weighted ability-level exposure index. They 
then summed this “weighted ability-level AI exposure” index “across all 
abilities in an occupation” (p. 2201) and used this sum to indicate the 
relative exposure to AI across industries. Examples of high exposure 
occupations included genetic counselors and financial examiners; 
examples of low exposure occupations included dancers and fitness 
trainers and aerobics instructors. Interestingly, the authors were also 
able to make predictions about which geographic regions were most 
likely to be impacted by AI integration in the workplace with urban 
regions showing much higher susceptibility than rural regions.
 
Pizzinelli, Panton, Tavares, and Cazzaniga (2023), offered a more 
nuanced view of automation risk by differentiating AI’s potential to 
substitute for labor from its potential to complement for labor. The 
authors gathered data for nine occupational categories in six countries. 
Before differentiating between substitution and complementarity, they 
first developed a measure of AI exposure, linking the 10 AI applications 
defined by Felten, Raj and Seamans (2021) to the 52 O*NET 
occupational abilities. They then used O*NET data to identify “job 
zones”— “groups of occupations characterized by similar levels of 
education, on-the-job training, and professional experience needed to 
perform the work” (p. 10). They also identified 11 O*NET job context 
items, which they combined with the job zones to identify six 
components likely to impact whether AI exposure would lead to 
substitution or complementation. Rather than generating a single metric 
of risk, Pizzinelli et al. (2023) identified four categories: “(i) High 
Exposure and High Complementarity; (ii) High Exposure and Low 
Complementarity; (ii) Low Exposure and High Complementarity; and (vi) 
Low Exposure and Low Complementarity” (p. 19). This led them to 
make such cross-country comparisons as this: “the US and UK host the 
largest proportion of workers exposed to AI. In addition, they also 
have the largest share of workers in occupations with both high 
exposure and high complementarity” (p. 20).
Another investigation (UK Department of Education, 2023, 
November).) incorporating Felten, Raj, and Seamans’ (2021) AI 
applications and the 52 O*NET occupational abilities eschewed the 
distinction between exposure and complementarity and simply looked at 
exposure to AI, with particular emphasis on large language modelling. 
This investigation focused on occupations in the United Kingdom. For 
all AI applications, the two occupational groups with the highest 
exposure were (1) management consultants and (2) financial managers 
and directors. For large language modelling specifically, the highest 
exposure groups were (1) telephone solicitors and (2) solicitors. There

was considerable overlap between the occupations identified in the top 
twenty for AI generally and those for large language models 
specifically, with eight occupations appearing in both lists.
Other AI-Related Research. Other investigators have deviated 
from the O*NET approach. Webb (2020) examined the “overlap 
between the text of job task descriptions and the text of patents” (p. 
1). He defined the set of artificial intelligence patents” as those that 
use certain keywords, such as “neural network”, in their titles or 
abstracts” (p. 13). He concluded that, “in contrast to software and 
robots, AI is directed at higher-skilled tasks” (p. 1). However, he also 
noted that other factors, such as complementarity and job creation, 
might mitigate substitution of technology for labor effects. 
Others have relied simply on survey data. Dun and Bradstreet 
(2019, January 8) surveyed attendees at AI World Conference and Expo 
in 2018 and found that “40 percent of respondents’ organizations” 
were “adding more jobs as a result of deploying AI within their 
business” and eight percent responded that their organizations were 
“cutting jobs due to AI implementation” (para. 1). Other respondents 
did not report an impact in either direction.
The World Economic Forum (2023) reported from its survey of 
803 organizations that employers “estimate that 44% of workers’ skills 
will be disrupted in the next five years” (p. 7). 
Artificial intelligence, a key driver of potential algorithmic 
displacement, is expected to be adopted by nearly 75% 
of surveyed companies and is expected to lead to high 
churn – with 50% of organizations expecting it to create 
job growth and 25% expecting it to create job losses. 
(World Economic Forum, 2023, p. 7)
Acemoglu, Autor, Hazell, and Restrepo (2022) went beyond the 
question of whether jobs were being replaced by AI to look at the 
impact of AI more broadly on employment. They used existing indices 
of “tasks and occupations that are most impacted by AI technologies” 
(p. 2) and determined an “establishment-level data set of AI activity 
based on the near-universe of US online job vacancy postings and their 
detailed skill requirements” from an available source “for the years 
2007 and 2010 through 2018” (p. 1). 
From these data, they were able to reach three conclusions: 
1)
There was a “rapid takeoff in AI vacancy postings starting in 
2010 and significantly accelerating around 2015-2016” (p. 2).

2)
AI exposure” was “associated with both a significant decline 
in some of the skills previously sought in posted vacancies 
and the emergence of new skills. This evidence bolsters the 
case that AI is altering the task structure of jobs, replacing 
some human-performed tasks while simultaneously generating 
new tasks accompanied by new skill demands” (p. 2)
3)
AI exposure was “associated with lower (non-AI and overall) 
hiring” (p. 3).
Despite these findings, they did not “detect any relationship 
between AI exposure and employment or wages at the occupation or 
industry level” (p. 26).
Albanesi, da Silva, Jimeno, Lamo, & Wabitsch (2023) similarly 
looked at macro effects of AI on employment. They used two indices 
to link exposure to AI to occupations. One was the Webb (2020) 
approach of determining the overlap between the text of job task 
descriptions and the text of patents. The other, described by Felten et 
al. (2018), involved linking O*NET abilities to the EFF AI Progress 
Measurement data. This approach was described above, as it was 
applied later by Felten, Raj, and Seamans (2021).
These indices were linked to a European Union labor force 
survey for the period 2011 to 2019, focusing on “employment shares 
and their variation over time by occupation” (p. 9). One finding was “a 
positive association between AI-enabled automation and changes in 
employment shares in the pooled sample” (p. 18) whether the Webb 
or the Felten et al. metric was used. 
Commenting on these results in a follow-up article, Albanesi, da 
Silva, Jimeno, Lamo, & Wabitsch (2023b) observed “AI-enabled 
automation is thus associated with employment increases in Europe – 
mostly for high-skill occupations and younger workers” (What Do the 
Results Say on the Impact of AI on Employment? section, para. 5). The 
shift in the conclusions from this study from those reported earlier by 
Acemoglu et al. (2022) and Webb (2022) were reflected in the title of 
the article, “Reports of AI ending human labour may be greatly 
exaggerated” (Albanesi et al., 2023b). 
Robotic-Related Research
A number of studies on tech-human replacement focused 
specifically on robots. Graetz and Michaels (2015, March) used a metric 
they called robot densification to examine the effect of utilization of 
robots on employment in 17 countries from 1993 to 2007. They found 
“no significant effect of robot densification on aggregate hours worked”

(p. 4).
Acemoglu and Restrepo (2017) compared their own measure of 
exposure to robots to employment by geographic computing zones in 
the United States during the same period as that examined by Graetz 
and Michaels, 1993 to 2007. They found the 
increase in the stock of robots (approximately one new 
robot per thousand workers from 1993 to 2007) reduced 
the employment to population ratio in a commuting zone 
with the average US exposure to robots by 0.37 
percentage points . . . relative to a commuting zone with 
no exposure to robots. . .. [T]hey imply that one more 
robot in a commuting zone reduces employment by 6.2 
workers. . .. (p. 40).
Petropoulos, Pichler, and Chiacchio (2017, 18 April) also used a 
localized approach in determining exposure to robots, employing a 
categorization that divides the European unit into 270 territorial units. 
Using this approach and available labor market data, they found that 
“one additional robot per thousand workers reduces the employment 
rate by 0.16-0.20 percentage points” (p. 1).
Acemoglu, LeLarge, and Restrepo (2020) studied “firm-level 
changes associated with robot adoption using data from France 
between 2010 and 2015” (p. 2). They found that firms that adopted 
robots increased overall employment as they increased their 
productivity, but because this expansion came at the expense of their 
competitors, the effect on overall employment was negative.
Chung and Lee (2023, March 1), like Acemoglu and Restropo 
(2017), examined robotic and employment changes by computing zones. 
They considered changes” over every 5-year period between 2005 and 
2016” (p. 292). They found that “robot exposure reduces employment 
in the earlier periods but augments employment in the more recent 
periods” (p. 290). They attributed this changing pattern primarily to 
changes in the auto industry,” in which digitization and automation 
have not only increased labor productivity but also created new tasks” 
(p. 290). 
Conclusions
We have reviewed a number of research findings to address 
the question: how many military personnel will be replaced by 
advancements in technology? The findings suggest that this question 
can be divided into a number of sub-questions:

1.
What occupations, or tasks within occupations, can be replaced 
by technology?
2.
How quickly are such replacements likely to occur?
3.
What new tasks or occupations will be needed to ensure this 
technology is optimally utilized?
4.
What other new tasks or occupations will emerge as a result 
of technological changes?
5.
Will the number of personnel replaced by technology exceed 
the number of new personnel added as a result of technological 
changes? If so, to what extent?
6.
What kinds of occupations are most exposed to technological 
changes, and in which direction?
What occupations, or tasks within occupations, can be replaced 
by technology? Much of the most systematic research on this question 
has focused on skills and abilities required to perform the tasks within 
an occupation. The availability of detailed skills and abilities information 
from O*NET makes this a feasible approach. However, the 
methodologies used to link skills and abilities data to the question of 
replacement vary considerably from study to study, and have, as a 
consequence, produced varying results. Despite these variations, the 
research consistently indicates a non-trivial potential for replacement 
across a wide range of occupations.
How quickly are such replacements likely to occur?
Tarraf et al. (2019) suggested that the implementation of new 
technology be considered in terms of three time frames: the near 
term (up to five years), the middle term (five to ten years), and the 
long term (beyond ten years). Determining when technology 
implementation will occur is challenging, and the studies considered 
here, when they addressed it at all, considered various time frames. 
The Defense Science Board (2017) examined which military occupations 
would be automatable “now or in the near future.” Lassebie and 
Quintini (2022), in their survey of AI experts, asked whether each of 
the O*NET skills and abilities, given current capabilities, could be 
automated in the next 5 to 20 years. McKinsey and Company (2017, 
p. viii) in their study published in 2017, provided estimates of 
automatability between that period and 2055—nearly forty years into 
the future.
Once it is determined that a human ability or skill or some 
other indicator of performance capability can be automated, several 
other criteria must be met in order for such automation can take 
place. McKinsey and Company (2017) identified five: (1) technical

feasibility, (2) cost of technology implementation, (3) current labor 
costs, (4) performance benefits, and (5) social and regulatory 
acceptance. In other words, a technically feasible solution must offer a 
cost advantage over the labor it replaces, provide equal or better 
performance quality, and not encounter insurmountable social and legal 
obstacles.
The criterion of social and regulatory acceptance requires special 
attention. Society may not be ready to accept replacement of certain 
human functions with unsupervised automation. Cazzaniga and 
co-authors (2024) noted that, even if tasks performed by judges could 
be automated, society would be reluctant to rely on a judicial ruling 
that had no human input. Similarly, an automatic weapon that can kill 
without human intervention raises significant ethical and regulatory 
concerns (Hart, 2020).
What New Tasks or Occupations Will Be Needed to Ensure this 
Technology Is Optimally Utilized? It should also be noted that, while 
automation may replace humans in some instances, it may also 
generate the need for new human jobs. In the case of artificial 
intelligence, these may include jobs to train AI systems, those to 
explain output of AI systems to others, and those to sustain AI 
systems (Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2018).
What other New Tasks or Occupations Will Emerge as a Result 
of Technological Changes? New technology may not only facilitate 
performance of existing tasks, it may also make the performance of 
new tasks possible, as found by Acemoglu, Autor, Hazell, and Restrepo 
(2022) and Chung and Lee (2023). 
 Performance of the new AI-related tasks may make the 
organization more productive, more efficient, or, in the case of the 
military, more lethal. When the organization is motivated to downsize, 
the generation of new work and new workers might be viewed as too 
expensive to contemplate. However, virtually every organization, 
whether civilian or military, is in a competitive situation. If 
technological changes lead to advantages that can only be achieved 
through increased personnel, the pressure to accept that outcome will 
be strong.
Will the Number of Personnel Replaced by Technology Exceed 
the Number of New Personnel Added as a Result of Technological 
Changes? If So, to What Extent? When jobs added are considered as 
well as jobs replaced, a mixed picture emerges. As noted above, 
Albanesi, da Silva, Jimeno, Lamo, & Wabitsch (2023) found AI-related 
employment increases, Acemoglu, Autor, Hazell, and Restrepo (2022) 
found no AI-related effect. Similarly, Graetz and Michaels (2015) found

no robotic-related effect. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2017), Acemoglu, 
LeLarge, and Restrepo (2020), and Petropoulos, Pichler, and Chiacchio 
(2017) found a negative robotic-related effect, whereas Chung and Lee 
(2023) found a negative robotic-related effect followed by a positive 
one.
Several of these studies have generated quantitative estimates of 
the overall employment effect. However, given the inconsistency of the 
findings, any such estimate should be viewed with a high degree of 
skepticism. Results vary according to the methodology used, the time 
period examined, and the population examined. It is difficult to draw 
any definitive conclusions from these findings. Perhaps the most 
interesting observation is that they cast doubt on the assumption that 
future automation will necessarily result in an overall reduction in 
employment. 
When considering the application of these studies to the military, 
some differences between the civilian environment and the military 
environment need to be noted. In the civilian world, there is often a 
more direct relationship between performance and employment: a better 
product by a civilian firm can lead to increased demand and, hence, 
more employment. In contrast, the military’s personnel requirements are 
constrained by the perceived threat environment, budgetary considerations, 
and the recruiting environment. On February 27, 2024, Baldor reported 
that: 
 
The U.S. Army is slashing the size of its force by about 
24,000, or almost 5%, and restructuring to be better able 
to fight the next major war, as the service struggles with 
recruiting shortfalls that made it impossible to bring in 
enough soldiers to fill all the jobs. (para. 1)
While the U.S. is planning new technologies and new doctrine 
for imagined futures in 2030 and 2040, the nature of the threat 
environment is constantly shifting. The war in Ukraine has been viewed 
as providing a “war lab for the future” (Bergengruen, 2024, February 
28, p. 31). The full implications of this war and the war in Gaza for 
the future battlefield will not be known until well into the future; 
meanwhile, plans for an incompletely known future go forward. 
The culture of the U.S. Army also needs to be considered. It 
has embraced AI and is moving toward automation on many fronts. 
However, it is a person-centric organization and may be more inclined 
to place limits on its dependence on technology than some other 
organizations. Speaking as Vice Chief of the Army, General James 
McConville observed:

at the end of the day, it’s about the Army’s Soldiers. 
There will always be a Soldier in the loop in anything we 
do. The technology is there to help them do their jobs, 
not to replace them. Soldiers are our most important 
asset. (Dilanian & Howard, 2018, p. 19)
What Kinds of Occupations Are Most Exposed to Technological 
Changes, and in which Direction? The studies examined did not provide 
a basis for an occupation-by-occupation analysis. However, they perhaps 
did reveal were insights about the kinds of occupations or skills most 
exposed to automation.” Some have suggested that, unlike other forms 
of automation, exposure to AI might be associated with high skill 
occupations. In terms of cognitive skills, genetic counselors and financial 
examiners, found to be high AI exposure occupations in Felten, Raj and 
Seamans’ (2021) study, might be considered in the high skills category, 
while dancers and fitness trainers and aerobic instructors, examples of 
low AI exposure occupations, might be considered to be less skilled. 
Similarly, the UK Department of Education (2023) identified 
management consultants and financial managers and directors as high 
exposure occupations and sports players and roofers, roof tilers and 
slaters as low exposure occupations. 
However, like everything else associated with AI, the picture is 
not so simple. Albanesi et al. (2023), in examining employment effects 
by skill level, found increases in employment only at the high skilled 
level. The skills or abilities identified Frey and Osborne (2017) identified 
as “bottlenecks” to automation--perception and manipulation, creativity, 
and social intelligence—cannot easily be said to represent attributes 
associated with the low skilled. Similarly, the five skills or abilities 
judged least automatable by the AI judges in the Lassebie and Quintini 
(2022) study-- management of personnel resources, complex problem 
solving, negotiation, social perceptiveness, and technology 
design—similarly do not suggest low skills.
McKinsey and Company (2017) similarly characterized machines 
as lacking certain highly sophisticated skills: 
They are not yet good at putting knowledge into context, 
let alone improvising. They have little of the common 
sense that is the essence of human experience and 
emotion. They struggle to operate without a pre-defined 
methodology. They are far more literal than people, and 
poor at picking up social or emotional cues. Sarcasm and 
irony pass them by. They generally cannot detect whether 
a customer is upset at a hospital bill or a death in the

family, and for now, they cannot answer “What do you 
think about the people in this photograph?” or other 
open-ended questions. They can tell jokes without really 
understanding them. They don’t yet feel humiliation, fear, 
pride, anger, or happiness. They also struggle with 
disambiguation, unsure whether a mention of the word 
“mercury” refers to a planet, a metal, or the winged god 
of Roman mythology. (pp. 26-27) 
Although AI is celebrated for its unique capability to accomplish 
certain very complex and difficult tasks, it has also been found to be 
an effective tool for performing lower skilled tasks as well. This utility 
is often overlooked, but is nonetheless valuable. As already observed in 
this paper, Daniels (2023, November 13, para. 3), noted its use in the 
Army Reserve for “routine, labor-intensive tasks. . . such as copying, 
pasting and moving files.”

Research Design
The question of replacing military personnel has been driven by 
advances in AI and robotics. These advancements have been so 
dramatic that they suggest traditional concepts of automation may no 
longer apply. Generative artificial intelligence in particular has been 
viewed as sui generis—something that we must make new rules for 
understanding. This investigation is rooted in the belief that, whether 
we are considering artificial intelligence or robotics, the broader 
umbrella of automation still applies. While these particular applications 
may have accelerated the process beyond anything seen before, they 
still share one element common to all forms of automation: the 
replacement or augmentation of human capabilities with non-human 
capabilities.
In this investigation, we have pursued three paths, each related 
to factors influencing performance. The first involves the skills and 
abilities needed to produce some performance outcome. To what 
degree is each automatable? The second involves the work context in 
which performance takes place. Which contextual factors facilitate or 
inhibit automation? The third involves work training and experience. 
Training and experience enhance the skills and abilities that are needed 
for performance to advance to a higher level. Presumably, the more 
time needed to learn from training or experience to qualify for a job, 
the more complex the job is, and thus, the more difficult it is to 
automate that job. The measures associated with each of these paths 
will now be considered.
Two automatability metrics were generated within this study. 
The first combined a composite of skills and abilities scores with a 
composite of work context variables. The combination of these 
composites yielded what might be considered in some respects to be 
an “absolute” metric because of the nature of the available data. The 
second metric added a composite of experience and training scores to 
the skills/abilities and work context measures. Because the experience 
and training scores could not be converted to an absolute scale, this 
metric was used only for comparative purposes. 
Data Sources
Skills, Abilities, and Work Context
Occupational Information Network (O*NET). The O*NET is an 
unparalleled source of information about jobs in the United States. It is 
an online source with six sections: (1) Work Characteristics, (2) Worker 
Requirements, (3) Experience Requirements, (4) Occupational

Requirements, (5) Workforce Characteristics, and (6) Occupation-Specific 
Information (Tippins & Hilton, 2010).
The O*NET covers over 900 civilian occupations. Data are 
continually updated through a series of data collection cycles. The last 
reported cycle (Burgoyne & Reeder, 2023b) covered 90 occupations. 
Military occupations are linked to civilian occupations based on 
similarity of work performed, knowledge base, and title similarity 
(Dahlke, Putka, Shewach, & Lewis, 2022).
Data Extracted from O*NET for Purposes of this Investigation
 
Skills and Abilities Data. Eight trained occupational analysts 
provide importance and level ratings on 35 skills (Burgoyne & Reeder, 
2023b) and 52 abilities Burgoyne & Reeder, 2023a) with respect to 
each occupation. 
Work Context Data. Ideally, a minimum of 15 incumbents in 
each occupation periodically completes a questionnaire describing the 
work context in which workers perform (Tippins & Hilton, 2010). The 
work context questionnaire was designed to cover the following six 
areas: Physical Work Conditions, Structural Job Characteristics, 
Performance Work Output, Affective Response, Physical Response, and 
Psychological Response. A factor analysis of the 57-item job context 
questionnaire generated seven factors (Strong, Jeanneret, McPhail, 
Blakley, & D’Egidio, 1999), two of which are of particular interest for 
this investigation: Personal and Interpersonal Relations, and Structural 
and Machine Operations. Based primarily on factor weightings, the 
following seven items were initially selected from these factors for 
investigation:
Managerial and Interpersonal Factor
1)
Frequency of face to face interactions
2)
Coordination with others
3)
Freedom to make decisions
4)
Responsibility for outcomes and results
Structural and Machine Factor
1)
Importance of repeating tasks
2)
Degree of automation
3)
Structured versus unstructured
In the course of this investigation, two additional items were 
added: (1) time spent on repetitive motions and (2) consequence of 
error. Each of the total of nine items received a score of 0 to 4, with 
0 representing no automatability and 4 representing the highest degree

of automatability. 
Appendix A presents each of the nine items and the range of 
possible responses.
Skills and Abilities Automatability Data 
Lassebie and Quintini (2022) surveyed 20 experts in the fields of 
artificial intelligence and robotics, asking whether each of the O*NET 
skills and abilities, given current capabilities, could be automated in the 
next 5 to 20 years. Responses were scored using a range from 0 (no) 
to 5 (yes, in all contexts). 
Work Training and Experience Data
Rationale. Work training and experience are expected to 
influence automatability in three ways. First, as jobs become complex 
—requiring specialized knowledge, advanced reasoning, or the effective 
coordination of multiple tasks—the difficulty of implementing 
automation to replace human labor increases. Consequently, the 
likelihood of such implementation occurring within a given time 
diminishes. Indicators of complexity are likely to be associated with the 
need for greater training or experience.
Second, jobs requiring greater training and experience also tend 
to carry higher levels of responsibility and prestige. These roles are 
more likely to be perceived as requiring some level of human 
involvement.
Third, incumbents in jobs which requiring greater training and 
experience are likely to be skilled in leveraging automation to enhance 
their own performance. In these cases, automation complements, rather 
than replaces, human labor. As articulated by Pizzinelli, Panton, and 
Tavares (2023, p. 10): “occupations with longer periods of required 
professional development would have greater ability to integrate AI 
knowledge into their training programs and thus equip workers with 
complementary skills.”
Measures. Two types of training and experience measures were 
used. The first concerned indirect training obtained prior to job 
placement, primarily through education. A metric was needed that 
could equate different types of such training in terms of its perceived 
value to the Army. This value, in turn, would be an indirect estimate 
of the difficulty of replacing this training through automation.
To develop a metric applicable across different types of

expertise and Army personnel (enlisted soldiers, warrant officers, and 
commissioned officers), Brogden and Taylor’s (1950) approach of 
combining multiple criteria into a single dollar value was used. The 
value the Army places upon the training and education required of a 
soldier or officer can be perceived by the amount they are willing to 
pay such an individual upon entry. This value, though indirect, is 
useful.
 
Three types of pay were considered: base pay, bonus, and 
incentive pay. To determine base pay, pay scales were obtained for 
commissioned officers, warrant officers, and enlisted soldiers at entry 
(Department of Defense, 2024b). The base pay for an enlisted soldier 
was anchored at the value “1.” 
For some specialties requiring a higher level of experience, 
soldiers started at a higher base. For example, a Recruiter (79R) starts 
at the sergeant level, and is thus accorded a value of 1.6. The same 
holds for all warrant officers, with the exception of Rotary Wing 
Aviator (153A), which does not require previous experience. A Career 
Counselor must be a staff sergeant, and thus is accorded a value of 
1.9. A Chief Signal NCO (25X) must be a sergeant major or a 
command sergeant value, which equates roughly to a value of 2.2. 
Commissioned officers, receiving approximately twice the pay of 
an entering enlisted soldier, started from base “2.” Examples of 
positions requiring a higher rank and thus associated with higher levels 
include Latin America Foreign Officer (48B, value 2.38) and United 
States Military Academy Professor of English (47C, value 2.57). Medical 
officer positions, requiring medical degrees and licenses, were 
associated with a higher entry rank and salary, raising their base level 
to a “3.” These positions also receive disproportionate incentive and 
bonus pay.
Bonus pay is given to applicants in certain enlisted or officer 
specialties. Incentive pay, associated with certain specialties, was 
calculated as a proportion of total pay and summed with the base pay 
metric. Incentive pay was calculated annually, while bonus pay was 
pro-rated over four years, which best represented the length of time 
enlisted soldiers and officers would serve on Active Duty in their first 
term.
Because an officer at entry received roughly twice that amount, 
they were awarded the number “2.” The pay of medical officers 
translated to the value “3,” For military occupational specialties (MOS) 
that were staffed by noncommissioned officers, the number varied from 
1.6 to 2.2, depending on the rank needed in those MOS. Similarly,

officer specialties that could only be filled by incumbents at a 
particular rank were associated with a number equivalent to the salary 
at that rank.
The second type of pay is bonus pay. The Army is willing to 
pay a bonus to applicants who access in certain enlisted or officer 
specialties. The third type of pay is incentive pay, which again is 
associated with certain specialties. Each of these additional types were 
calculated as a proportion of total pay and summed with the base pay 
metric. Incentive pay was calculated on an annual basis, while bonus 
pay was pro-rated across four-years, which best represented the length 
of time enlisted soldiers and officers would serve on Active Duty in 
their first term. Information about various types of incentive and bonus 
pay for particular enlisted and officer specialties can be found on two 
military websites: goarmy.com and Defense Finance and Accounting 
Service (2024).
Two other measures of experience and training were collected. 
One was initial specialty training after entry. For enlisted soldiers, the 
measure is number of weeks in Advanced Individual Training (AIT), 
which the soldier receives after Basic Combat Training (BCT). For some 
specialties, BCT and AIT are combined in One Station Unit Training. For 
these specialties, we calculated AIT as the difference between OSUT 
training and the number of weeks other soldiers spend in BCT. For 
officers, the measure is Officer Basic Course.
The second additional measure was number of required years 
of education prior to entry. In general, this measure is confounded 
with base pay, since only commissioned officers are required to 
complete college. However, since medical specialties require 
post-graduate education, the metric used here was number of years of 
such education as well as years associated with required additional 
training. 
Sample
The sample was drawn from the full population of Army 
non-combat jobs—enlisted soldiers, commissioned officers and warrant 
officers. The first step for drawing a sample of jobs from that 
population was to eliminate jobs with no civilian counterparts, since 
the O*NET data were based on civilian jobs. The second step was to 
eliminate jobs with either no or incomplete skill or ability data. The 
third step was to eliminate jobs with either no or incomplete work 
context data. Finally, jobs were eliminated with no experience or 
training data.

As the project progressed, updates to the O*NET data base 
resulted in certain civilian-military job connections being eliminated. 
Thus, some of the Army jobs initially included had to be dropped from 
the investigation. 
The sample of 149 Army jobs (62 enlisted, 27 warrant officer, 
and 60 commissioned officer) were those remaining after these 
elimination steps had been completed. As a basis for determining the 
representativeness of these jobs of the total population of Army jobs, 
job categories were used. These categories were drawn from the 
Department of Defense Occupational Conversion index (2001).
 
 Of the ten enlisted categories identified in this source, eight 
consisted basically of non-combat jobs. These eight categories 
represented approximately 73% of the active enlisted force in 2019 (by 
Occupational Area: 5.51% Electronics; 12.86% Communications; 8.66% 
Medical; 3% Other Technical; 14.36% Administrators;13.86 Electrical; 
2.5% Craftsman; 12.12% Supply). Each of the eight categories was 
represented in this research, as shown in Appendix B. The remaining 
two categories were (1) Infantry, Gun Crews, and Seamanship, and (2) 
Non-Occupational.
None of the nine commissioned officer categories consisted 
exclusively of combat jobs, although one, Tactical Operations, was 
heavily oriented towards combat. Tactical Operations jobs encompassed 
30.84% of the active Army force in 2019. Aside from general officers 
and a non-occupational category, the remaining officer job categories 
encompassed 67% of the commissioned officer force (7.81% Intelligence; 
14.57% Engineering and Maintenance; 7.82% Scientists and 
Professionals; 19.18% Medical; 7.3% Administration; and 10.73% Supply 
and Procurement (Department of Defense, 2019). The representation of 
these categories, along with Tactical Operations, in this research is 
shown in Appendix C. The concordance between warrant officer jobs 
and these categories is also shown in this appendix. 
In determining representativeness of the sample, it would also 
have been desirable to know the number of incumbents in these jobs 
relative to the total population of Army jobs. However, after a careful 
search, it was determined that this information was generally not 
available from official unclassified sources. There was some unofficial 
information that suggested that certain jobs were of relatively low 
density, such as the job of Army Astronaut or individual United States 
Military Academy jobs by content specialty. The former job was not 
included, and one job was chosen to represent the latter group. There 
was also unofficial data that suggested that certain jobs were relatively 
higher in density. For example, an Army Times article (Rempfer, 2019)

identified the ten MOS with the highest number of recruits in 2019. 
Three of these MOS (Military Police, Human Resources Specialist, and 
Motor Transport Operator) were included in the enlisted sample. 
However, beyond this information, the population density of particular 
jobs could not be ascertained.

Analyses and Results
Phase One: Calculation of Absolute Metric
As noted earlier, one automatability metric was based on a 
combination of a skills and abilities composite and a composite of 
work context variables. Because of the nature of the data associated 
with these data, this metric was described as an absolute one. This is 
the metric to be used to estimate a replacement ratio across all Army 
non-combat occupations. This section describes the generation of this 
metric and a description of the results obtained during the process of 
calculating it. 
Skills and Abilities Data
 
As noted above, 62 Army enlisted jobs, 27 warrant officer jobs, 
and 60 commissioned officer jobs which have O*NET skills and abilities 
data for comparable civilian jobs, were examined. The five most 
important skills and abilities for each job, based on occupational 
analyst ratings, were identified. 
Automatability ratings derived from the 20 experts in the 
Lassebie and Quintini (2022) study were assigned for each of these 
skills and abilities. 
Each of these skill and ability automatability ratings were 
multiplied by an importance value. This importance value was the raw 
importance value obtained from the O*NET database, entered as a 
percentage, divided by the average of the five raw skill or ability 
values for that job. The resulting quotient, representing a transformed 
importance value, was then multiplied by the raw automatability rating 
for that skill or ability. The product, becoming the transformed 
Skills/Ability automatability rating, was then entered into a calculation 
of the average of the transformed automatability values for the 
selected skills or abilities for that job. The averages thus generated for 
the transformed skill and transformed ability ratings were themselves 
averaged to generate the new automatability value for that job.

For the same 149 jobs for which skills and abilities data were 
obtained, work context data from the O*NET database for the nine 
items described above were also obtained. Scoring of the four items 
selected from the managerial and interpersonal factor were based on 
the expectation that greater interactions, greater coordination, greater 
freedom and greater responsibility are inversely associated with 
automatability. Scoring of the remaining items was based on the 
expectations that (1) job structure and repetition of tasks are both 
positively associated with automatability, (2) that tasks that are already 
highly automated are, by their nature, highly automatable, and (3) that 
more consequential tasks are negatively associated with automatability. 
Each of the Work Context items (the two repetition items were 
combined to form a single score) was expected to contribute to the 
overall automatability rating for each job. Correlational analyses were 
conducted to determine the viability of that approach. The sample of 
jobs used in this analysis were reduced from the original 149 to 94 so 
that no more than one Army job was associated with any particular 
civilian job. The automatability rating based on skills and abilities from 
O*NET and ratings from the items from the Work Context 
questionnaire are shown in Table 5.
The four items earlier identified as comprising the managerial 
and interpersonal factor, Frequency of face to face interactions; 
Coordination with others, Freedom to make decisions,
and Responsibility for outcomes and results, were highly intercorrelated, 
as Table 5 demonstrates.
Structure, which had been postulated as belonging to the 
Structural and Machine factor, did not fit well with Degree of 
Automation (r = .03, NS), although it fit somewhat better with 
Repetition (combination of two repetition variables with Structure, r= 
.21, NS). On the other hand, it did fit quite well with Face to Face 
interaction (r = .45, p<.001), Coordination (r= .40), Freedom to Make 
Decisions (r = .83, p<.001), and Responsibility for Outcomes (r = .32, 
p<.01). Thus, it was added to the Managerial and Interpersonal scale 
to form a single scale, leaving Automation and Repetition, which 
intercorrelated well (r = .48, p<.001) as occupying a separate scale, and 
Consequence of Error comprising a single-item scale. The removal of 
Structure from what was previously described Structural and Machine 
scale changed the nature of that scale, such that it now became just 
the Automation and Repetition scale.

Degree of Automation and Repetition. Degree of Automation, an 
indicator of the extent to which a job is already automated, was of 
particular interest. In determining which jobs would be most susceptible 
to future automation, current automation had to be a consideration, 
but in which direction? Would jobs that were already highly automated 
more likely to move further in that direction, or less likely?
As noted above, a composite of two items representing 
Repetition correlated at a highly significant level with Degree of 
Automation. The relationship suggested a simple dynamic. If a job 
could be broken down into individual repetitive tasks, it could more 
easily be automated than one which more typically involved novel 
tasks. Such a relationship could apply to artificial intelligence as easily 
as to other forms of automation. Artificial intelligence is highly 
sophisticated, but it involves training on available information. If a task 
is performed infrequently, then the information needed to properly 
perform that task is less likely to be available in the training set and 
the difficultly of using artificial intelligence as a substitute for human 
labor is likely to increase.
As shown in Table 5, none of the other Work Context variables 
correlated with Degree of Automation at a level above .14. The 
correlations between the Automation Score and the average score on 
the skills and abilities metric was an unimpressive .08, while that 
between the average of the two Repetition scores and skills and 
abilities was an even more unimpressive -.05. Neither of these 
values reached a level of significance at a probability level of .05. This 
reinforced the belief that the scale combining the Repetition Composite 
and the Degree of Automation scale provided a relatively independent 
source of variance in determining an overall automatability score.

Consequence of Error. In choosing whether or not to automate 
a function, consequences of error are particularly salient. Does one 
trust one’s self or automation more to avoid error? If the algorithms 
on which the automation depends are transparent, trust in their fidelity 
may not be a serious problem. However, as artificial intelligence 
algorithms become more complex and opaque, trust is not so easily 
obtained. This becomes particularly problematic to the extent 
consequences of error become more and more severe. Thus, perceived 
consequence of error was considered in this investigation to be a 
potential barrier to automation. 
For this research, an item measuring perceived consequence of 
error was scored, as were all Work Context items, such that lower 
scores were judged to represent low levels of potential automatability 
and high scores to represent high levels. For this item, this required 
reversing the original assigned score. Thus, “extremely serious” was 
assigned the lowest score and “not serious at all” the highest. Thus 
scored, the item Consequence of Error correlated -.05 with the average 
of skills and abilities (shown in Table 7), -.13 with Degree of 
Automation, both values failing to reach a level of significance at a 
probability of .05, and -.40 with the average of the two Repetition 
scores (p<.001).
The last finding is striking for both its magnitude and direction, 
and deserves comment. It should be noted that the Repetition scores 
were not reversed, so higher Repetition scores indicated judgments of 
higher importance of repetition and more repetitive actions. Thus, a 
positive correlation would indicate that more repetition was associated 
with less consequence of error. This might seem to make sense, but 
the negative correlation indicated the opposite was happening—more 
repetition was associated with higher consequence of error.

Phase Two: Calculation of Relative Metric
Automatability composites were developed for two purposes: (1) 
to generate an overall estimate of automatability across all Army 
non-combat jobs, and (2) to estimate the relative automatability of 
different Army jobs. Thus far, we have discussed the generation of the 
first metric, to provide an overall estimate of automatability. This 
metric includes skills, abilities, and work context variables. However, we 
have proposed another set of variables for consideration, involving 
work experience and training.
 Ideally, the work experience and training variables would have 
been included in generating the overall estimate However, because of 
the fundamental difference between the Experience and Training 
metrics and those associated with the other two composites, this 
approach was deemed to not be advisable.
The Skills and Abilities and Work Context measures, while 
subjective, were designed to elicit judgments that could be considered, 
in at some respects, of an absolute nature. While the Skills and 
Abilities measure generated relative judgments about the skills and 
abilities that were important to the performance job, these judgments 
were also linked to absolute judgments, ranging from not automatable 
to automatable in all contexts, about the automatability of these skills 
and abilities in the next five years. Similarly, the Work Context

Discussion
Overall Replacement Implications
The central objective of this investigation was to obtain an 
estimate of the replacement ratio for the United States Army military 
population given potential future automatability within a five to 
ten-year timeframe. 
Two automatability metrics were generated within this study. 
The first, considered in some respects to be an “absolute” metric, 
combined estimates of required skills and abilities with judgments on a 
number of work context parameters to estimate an absolute 
replacement ratio. The second, used only for comparative purposes, 
also considered experience and training, based on both direct and 
surrogate measures. As it turned out, the two metrics yielded almost 
identical results. The Experience and Training composite measure, once 
weighted inversely by variance, had minimal impact on the observed 
ratio.
An estimated ratio of .34 was obtained on the absolute scale. A 
ratio of .34 would imply that 34 out of every 100 jobs could be 
replaced by automation. However, to fully understand what this ratio 
means, we must examine this result more closely. 
Historically, automation waves in the military, such as the 
introduction of mechanized vehicles and advanced communication 
systems, have led to both job displacement and creation. 
Understanding these past transitions can provide valuable lessons for 
managing current and future changes.
Practical and Perceptual Considerations
First, it is important to clarify that the absolute estimated ratio 
obtained is not a prediction that 34 out of 100 jobs will be replaced. 
Even if this is an accurate estimate of replacement potential, an 
assumption that we will need to evaluate later in this section, there 
are a number of conditions that must be met before a potential 
replacement can be converted into an actual replacement. Some of 
these are practical; others are perceptual.
1.
Development of Automation: The automation vehicle must 
be developed. Saying that a job is automatable does not 
imply that the automation capability currently exists. 
Achieving such automation may require new equipment, new 
software, or a combination of both. In either case, a 
non-trivial developmental timetable window will be required. 
This timetable will likely incorporate time to execute a

procurement to obtain the new product, to develop a 
prototype of that product, to test the prototype, to conduct 
further development as needed, and, finally, to deliver the 
final product. Even if that process began today, the time required 
for full implementation might well exceed five years. Starting later 
would push implementation even further into the future.
2.
Cost-effectiveness: The automation must be cost-effective. A 
task may be automatable, but not necessarily more 
effectively or more cheaply performed by a machine. This 
involves both practical and perceptual considerations, as 
development will not proceed unless the final product is 
projected to be cost-effective. The McKinsey and Company 
(2017) analysis discussed earlier should be considered here.
3.
Trust in Automation: The automation must be trusted. Some 
functions may be so sensitive or consequential that humans 
hesitate to trust them to machines. This issue was addressed 
in part, but perhaps not completely in the present 
investigation by the use of the Consequence of Error item.
4.
Need for Back-ups: Automation systems require back-ups in 
case of failure. Software updates can introduce errors with 
disastrous consequences, as seen with the “CrowdStrike 
software bug “in July 2024, which “took down global IT 
infrastructure” (Ginsky, 2024). Malicious actors can also cause 
software systems to fail or otherwise malfunction. Without 
back-ups, such failures can disable existing systems for an 
indefinite period. To prevent or remedy such problems may 
require new labor inputs.
 
5.
Job Creation: Automation does not only replace jobs; it also 
creates them. Workers will be needed to supervise 
automation, interpret and utilize the information it provides, 
and to update the systems with new algorithms or 
equipment. In the case of AI, personnel will also be needed 
to train AI systems (Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2018). Further, as 
automation yields new capabilities, new personnel may be 
needed to fully exploit new opportunities.
The cumulative effect of all these factors is difficult to measure, 
but is probably considerable, particularly when new job creation is 
considered. It is not unreasonable to think the potential ratio of .34 
could be reduced by half or more in practice. It could even disappear 
entirely if improved performance made possible by new automated 
technology was prioritized over cost efficiency.

Notable Patterns
Other findings deserve comment, either for what they indicate 
about the credibility of the approach used or the manner in which 
certain job characteristics relate to automatability.
One notable pattern concerns the relative automatability of 
enlisted versus officer jobs. Enlisted and officer jobs are often 
examined separately due to fundamental differences such as level of 
responsibility and prior education requirements. Therefore, examining 
them using common standards is unusual, and the results from such 
an analysis must be viewed with caution.
It is not surprising to find that estimates of overall 
automatability, based on skills/abilities and work context, were lower 
for officer jobs than for enlisted jobs. However, the fact that the 
difference was only three points is somewhat surprising. This suggests 
that, in some cases, job-specific factors are more important than 
factors associated with overall job status. 
Low Automatability Enlisted Jobs
Two enlisted specialties are indicative of this pattern. The Army 
military occupational specialty 15P, Aviation Operations Specialist, had 
the lowest enlisted automatability rating on both the absolute and 
comparative metrics. This job involves scheduling and dispatching 
tactical aircraft missions and responding to emergencies (see 
goarmy.com). The automatability ratings for the comparable civilian job 
were particularly low with respect to the dimensions Consequence of 
Error (.21 versus a mean of 1.68 across all jobs studied here), 
Freedom to Make Decisions (.21 versus .74), Structure (.35 versus .78), 
and Face to Face interaction (.14 versus .32).
The other specialty, Practical Nursing Specialist (68C), had the 
second lowest rating for non-supervisory enlisted jobs on both criteria. 
It involves “performing preventive, therapeutic, and emergency nursing 
care”(Department of the Army, 2024). This nursing job had 
automatability scores at least one standard deviation below the mean 
on the following variables: Face to Face interaction (.32 versus .06, SD 
= .23), Coordinate with Others (.56 versus 1.12, .SD = .43), and Skills 
and Abilities (1.6 versus 1.98, SD = .31).

The Ubiquity of Medical Jobs
The dominance of medical jobs in the list of those least 
automatable is particularly striking. Indeed, six of the seven jobs 
identified as most automatable on both consolidated criteria are 
medical positions. This is notable given the increasing promise of 
automation to perform even some medical tasks traditionally managed 
by humans, as discussed earlier in this paper. 
In part, this can be attributed to an over-sampling of medical 
jobs, which make up a much higher proportion of our sample than of 
the overall military population. Although this over-representation is 
accounted for in the calculation of overall ratings, which are weighted 
to mitigate such effects, it does help explain why so many medical 
jobs appear in the least automatable officer jobs list. 
When comparing medical jobs to other occupational categories, 
a much more nuanced picture emerges. This picture reveals a notable 
difference between officer and enlisted job automatability. For officers, 
jobs in the health care category are approximately two points less 
automatable than the average across all officer jobs (.30 versus .32) 
when automatability is measured in terms of skills and abilities and 
work context, although the average for Administration jobs is even 
lower (.28). Among enlisted soldiers, medical jobs were found to be 
slightly more automatable on average (.36 versus .35) than other jobs 
on the same criterion.
An examination of the nature of officer versus enlisted medical 
specialties helps explain this difference. Officer medical jobs, such as 
neurology, psychiatry, and anesthesiology, tend to be highly specialized, 
requiring skills that take many years to develop, and knowledge that 
takes years to obtain. Conversely, enlisted medical jobs often involve 
more routine and mechanical tasks, such as the job of optical 
laboratory specialist (68H). Soldiers in this specialty handle prescriptions 
and make prescription lenses (see goarmy.com). This job is rated as 
automatable as any of the Army jobs considered, whether or not 
Experience and Training is considered.
The Aviation Jobs Conundrum
The inclusion of warrant officers in this investigation recognizes 
their special status in the military. “Warrant officers serve at all 
echelons as. . . specialized experts, integrators, managers and trainers. . .” 
(Department of the Army, 2022, p. 1-5). Although warrant officers were 
grouped with commissioned officers for many purposes in this research, 
they tend to serve more specialized functions than other officers.

Aviation jobs were particularly conspicuous among the warrant 
officer jobs included here. Ten of the 27 warrant officer jobs were for 
aviators. There are reasons why one may not expect warrant officer 
aviation jobs to be highly automatable. Qualification standards suggest 
skill demands for these jobs are high. Warrant officer aviators must 
receive an above average score on the enlisted accession Armed 
Services Vocational Aptitude Battery (ASVAB) General Technical (GT) 
composite, which combines scores on Word Knowledge, Paragraph 
Comprehension, and Arithmetic Reasoning tests (Department of Defense, 
2024a). They must also receive a passing score on the Selection 
Instrument for Flight Training (SIFT, US Army Recruiting Command, n.d.) 
composed of a number of cognitive, spatial and information tests 
(Ingurgio & Crawford, 2017) and complete an extensive flight training 
requirement (US Army Recruiting Command, n.d.). 
 
However, all ten of the aviator warrant officer jobs were 
among the twelve most automatable jobs in terms of skills and abilities 
for all officers, including both warrant and commissioned. Operation 
monitoring, control precision, near vision, and far vision, all among the 
most highly rated skills and abilities in terms of automatability for both 
rotary wing and fixed wing aviators, and are also among the skills 
rated most automatable by the experts in the Lassebie and Quintini 
(2022) study. Operation monitoring was classified by Mumford, Peterson 
and Childs (1999) as a technical skill, while control precision was 
classified as a psychomotor ability and near vision and far vision were 
categorized as sensory abilities by Fleishman, Costanza and 
Marshall-Mies (1999). Such skill and ability ratings tended to be rated 
as more automatable than more cognitively-oriented skills and abilities 
by the Lassebie and Quintini (2022) experts.
The two fixed wing warrant officer aviator jobs, Fixed Wing 
Aviator (155A) and C-12 Pilot Warrant Officer (155E) received among 
the highest automatability scores on the Automation/Repetition Work 
Context dimension. These same two jobs also received overall 
automatability ratings which placed them in a tie for 124th out of 149 
jobs on the comparative metric. The other eight other Warrant Officer 
jobs ended up the mid-range of jobs on this metric, a relatively 
unremarkable finding.
From a practical standpoint, what would it mean to replace a 
pilot with automation? Army aircraft typically have two pilots, so that 
one can take over if the other is incapacitated. “Army aircraft are 
designed as two-pilot aircraft. . . because we operate in harsh 
environments, performing complex missions” (Detachment 10, 2019, 
para. 9). Elimination of one pilot would sacrifice the safety of 
redundancy. However, to the extent unmanned aircraft could replace or

team up with manned aircraft to perform certain activities, some 
reduction in the need for Army pilots of fixed wing aircraft may be 
possible. 
Research Limitations
Now let us consider limitations of this research. This study rests 
on judgments which have yet to be fully validated. This includes 
judgments regarding the relationship between particular skills and 
abilities and automatability, although these judgments do have the 
advantage of being rendered by experts. A validation of these 
judgments against objective measures of automatability has yet to be 
conducted. 
Additionally, judgments about the relationship between certain 
work context variables and automatability are generally unvalidated 
against an external criterion. However, the relationship between 
Repetition and Level of Automation can be interpreted as 
demonstrating that the more a job involves repetitive actions and the 
more repetition is an important aspect of a job, the more likely it is 
to be automated. This is a relationship that has been largely, if not 
completely, neglected in previous automatability research, and which 
deserves more attention in the future.
Another limitation concerns the sample. The sample is 
necessarily limited to those jobs which have civilian counterparts. This 
not only excludes enlisted combat jobs but others as well that are 
unique to the military. Fortunately, every job category except for the 
enlisted combat category was represented by at least three jobs in this 
research. However, since information on the population size of each 
job was unavailable, there is a concern that there may have been 
insufficient coverage of at least some of these categories.
It is important to consider how the results from this research 
may generalize to combat jobs. This is particularly true for enlisted 
jobs, which were not represented at all in the category that 
incorporated combat jobs. The officer jobs in the Tactical Operations, 
which included fixed wing and rotary wing pilots, could be considered 
to have a combat role. These jobs, with an automatability ratio of .35, 
deviated only slightly from the combined ratio of .34 for officers and 
enlisted, but was notably above the ratio of .32 for all jobs in the 
officer category.
A broader question concerns the legitimacy of using data from 
civilian jobs to make judgments about military jobs. To address this 
question, one must consider the most fundamental differences between

the two types of jobs. Military personnel are considered to be on duty 
24 hours a day; civilians are generally only considered to be on the 
job for a limited portion of the day. Military personnel are generally 
more exposed to danger than civilians. Military personnel are under 
contract and have less job flexibility than civilians. Military personnel 
work in a highly structured, regimented, hierarchical organization; 
civilians tend to work in a more fluid environment. Military personnel 
often work in field environments and in groups, particularly those in 
combat jobs.
The overall net impact of these differences is unclear. For 
certain military jobs, interpersonal factors may weigh more heavily than 
for typical civilian jobs, which might imply less automation. More 
structure implies more automation. Danger might suggest either more 
automation to replace humans in harm’s way with robots or less 
automation to facilitate individual flexibility and spontaneity in 
fast-changing, ambiguous, and fluid environments. There does not seem 
to be an overriding factor which would clearly drive automation in one 
direction or another for either group relative to the other.
Future Research
Automatability research has been hampered by the lack of a 
true criterion. Theories of what factors affect automatability have yet 
to show convincing cause-effect relationships. At the same time, 
conducting planned experiments with manipulations designed to test 
such relationships would be difficult and time-consuming to conduct. 
In this research, we had the benefit of data which could 
retrospectively suggest relationships. We had judgments of the degree 
of automation in certain jobs and judgments of factors which might be 
associated with that automation. The strong relationship between 
repetition and automation stood out among those observed. 
It must be recognized that not all automation is equal. 
Generative AI has progressed far beyond earlier automation 
developments, and has expanded the understanding of AI capabilities. 
These capabilities are not limited to simple repetition. Nevertheless, 
repetition is a component of learning, even if not the only component. 
The design of this research does not enable fully a 
determination of whether the relationship between repetition and 
automation was a causal one, but the idea that it could be is 
compelling, as discussed earlier. Further investigation of the link 
between repetition and automation would seem to be advisable.

The relationship between skills and abilities and automatability 
also deserves further investigation. The ratings of automatability 
obtained by Lassebie and Quintini (2022) provides an excellent starting 
point, but additional judgments and verification of such judgments 
would be highly useful.
The role of experience and training is another area in need of 
further exploration. What kind of required experience and training 
makes a job resistant to automation and what kind does not? Does 
the accumulation of factual information or the development of 
cognitive skills constitute a benefit that cannot easily be replaced by 
automation? To what extent is training of manual tasks related to 
automatability?
Moreover, rapidly evolving technology could alter current 
estimations of automatability. Ongoing research is needed to keep pace 
with these advancements. Ethical and legal implications must also be 
considered, especially in automating roles involving combat and 
life-or-death decisions, which could encounter significant legal barriers.
The psychological impact on military personnel whose roles 
might be automated, and the social implications for military culture 
and cohesion, must also be examined. Automation could affect morale 
and the perception of military service. Additionally, the challenges 
related to integrating automated systems with existing military 
infrastructure, ensuring interoperability between human personnel and 
automated systems, need to be addressed.
A thorough cost-benefit analysis is essential, considering 
long-term maintenance and support costs for automated systems 
compared to human labor. Future research should focus on addressing 
current gaps in knowledge, including longitudinal studies to observe the 
impact of automation over time and cross-disciplinary research to 
incorporate insights from technology, military science, and human 
factors.
These questions only scratch the surface of what additional 
research is needed. Questions of automatability are complex, involving 
variations of types of automation, types of skills, abilities, tasks, 
experiences, interactions between skills, abilities, tasks and jobs, various 
approaches to task completion, various types of contextual variables, 
comparability between human capabilities and machine capabilities, and 
so much more. To fully address all the complexities involved would 
require an ambitious research program lasting decades, during which 
time technological advantages might fundamentally change the nature 
of both the questions being asked and the answers themselves. In the

meantime, we can move forward in an incremental fashion, answering 
questions to the extent existing data and resources allow. This 
investigation is but one small step in that direction.
